methods: Panel ARDL pooled mean group (PSS 1999), ARDL(1,1,1,1,1)

theme_confirmed: S (social sustainability: tourism and income equality; equality proxied by education expenditure per capita)
setting: 6 GCC countries: UAE, Bahrain, Oman, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia (panel)
data_source: World Bank WDI (tourism receipts, government effectiveness), Ministries of Finance (education expenditure), UNCTAD (FDI), UN Tourism/UNWTO (international arrivals)
period: 2014Q1-2023Q4 (abstract, intro, conclusion); methods section states 2014Q1 to 2020Q4
outcome_variables: EDU (education expenditure per capita, proxy for income equality)
methods: CSD tests (Breusch-Pagan LM, Pesaran scaled LM, bias-corrected scaled LM, Pesaran CD)

E.dependent_variable: EDU (log education expenditure per capita, proxy for income equality)

its lagged value (∆TOU(−1)) shows a positive and significant impact at the 5% level (p.18)
tourism revenue has a negative but not significant impact on income equality in the short run (p.18)

Tourist arrivals (TRV) exert no meaningful influence in either the current or lagged periods (p.18)

Period inconsistency: methods say 2014Q1 to 2020Q4, elsewhere 2014Q1-2023Q4; 218 observations vs 6 x 40 quarters = 240. Quarterly frequency claimed although sources (WDI, WGI) are typically annual; no interpolation method described. Text refers to GDP and TRADE (Table 5 text; discussion says 'GDP per capita emerged as the most significant long-term determinant') but neither is in the model or tables. CIPS table: TOU2 and FDI reported stationary at level while text says I(1). Pesaran CD for FDI (p=0.558) and GI (p=0.341) not significant, contrary to text claim all variables exhibit CSD. Long-run regressors labelled DLITA/DLTR (difference notation) though described as long-run elasticities. Bounds F = 8.705619 is below the 1% I(1) bound in Table 6 (8.803) but above the 1% I(1) bound in Table 7 (7.52); text claims significance at 5% and 10%. Observation count inconsistent (38 vs n=40). Conclusion: 1% increase in TR decreases CO2 by 0.15%, 1% increase in ITA increases CO2 by 0.24%. CO2 is total national emissions; aviation not discussed.

theme_confirmed: S (tourism-environment-health nexus: CO2, PM2.5, life expectancy)
setting: Italy, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye (separate country-level time series)
data_source: EDGAR (CO2, PM2.5), WDI (life expectancy, real GDP), STATISTA and UNWTO (tourist arrivals), BP (petroleum consumption)

E.estimator: Fourier-augmented VAR (FVAR) and Fourier Granger causality (no cointegration found, so no long-run estimates)
tourism_variables: TR (number of international tourist arrivals, proxy for religious tourism)
E.dependent_variable: COt vector (CO2 emissions) and PMt vector (PM2.5); also LE, TR, PC, Y vectors

key_results.evidence: the parameters for TRt−1 and TRt−2 are 0.236273 and 0.293544, and are significant at the 5% level of significance (p.9)
the parameters for TRt−1 and TRt−2 are 0.236273 and 0.293544, and are significant at the 5% level of significance (p.9)
accumulated long-run response of COt to tourism as 0.236273 + 0.293544 = 0.529817 (p.9)
Table 6 (p.10), TRt-1 row, COt column: 0.013429 ** (2.22086)
Table 6 (p.10), TRt-2 row, COt column: 0.147423 ** (2.22517)
Table 7 (p.11), TRt−1 row, COt column: 0.183585 *** (3.01162)
Table 7 (p.11), TRt−2 row, COt column: 0.204643 *** (3.14716)
a 1% point increase in TR leads to an accumulated effect of 0.387% point increase in COt (p.12)

key_results.variable: TR -> CO and TR -> PM Granger causality (all three countries)
key_results.evidence: The results indicate unilateral causal links for all countries from TR to PM and to CO (p.12)

out_of_sample_forecast.evidence: No forecasting reported; empirical analysis 'proceeds in three stages' of unit root, FVAR estimation and Fourier Granger causality (p.8)

E1_unit_root_tests.evidence: Fourier unit root tests were conducted, and the results are presented in Table 3 ... indicating that all series are I(1) processes (p.8)

E2_cointegration_or_long_run_test.evidence: The Johansen cointegration test indicates no cointegration for all variables in all the countries examined (p.8)

E3_structural_breaks.evidence: The model incorporates Fourier terms to control for structural breaks and is particularly advantageous for datasets with short time periods (p.8)

E4_cross_sectional_dependence_or_heterog.evidence: Separate FVAR estimations per country: 'The FVAR estimation results are presented in Tables 5–7 for the separate countries' (p.9)

E5_endogeneity_or_omitted_variables_addr.evidence: The FVAR model provides insights into the statistical significance and magnitude of the effects. The method handles endogeneity and feedback (p.8)

E6_diagnostics_stability.evidence: Tables 5–7 'Diagnostics' report only A.R2, F, LL, AIC, SC; no residual autocorrelation, heteroskedasticity or stability tests reported

E7_data_source_and_period.evidence: The dataset comprises annual data for 1975–2019 on CO2 emissions, air quality measured as PM2.5, religious tourism measured as international tourist arrivals, real GDP and petroleum consumption (p.6)

notes: No cointegration found, so no long-run coefficients; the 'accumulated long-run response' figures (Italy 0.529817, Türkiye 0.387) are sums of lagged VAR coefficients computed by the authors. Model equations (3)-(8) are written in first differences with an ecm term, but ecm is dropped given no cointegration. Tourist arrivals used as a proxy for religious tourism (no religious-tourism data). Fourier unit root critical values not reported in Table 3. Sample ends 2019 to exclude COVID-19. Some Granger-causality summaries in text (e.g., TR->CO for all countries) are drawn from Table 8 sign patterns.

theme_confirmed: S (sustainability and innovation as drivers of tourism/hotel recovery; tourism is the dependent variable, sustainability indicators are regressors)
data_source: UNWTO, World Bank WDI, Jordan Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, Global Innovation Index, Environmental Performance Index; dataset archived on Zenodo
methods: Fixed-effects regression with INN x SUS interaction
Random effects, CO2 proxy and lagged TRI robustness

E.estimator: Fixed-effects regression (STATA 17) on single-country annual series
tourism_variables: Tourism Recovery Index (dependent variable; built from arrivals and hotel occupancy relative to 2019)

key_results.evidence: Table 3 (p.126): Innovation Indicators (INN) 0.41 0.09 4.56 0.001**
Table 3 (p.126): Sustainability Indicators (SUS) 0.34 0.12 2.83 0.032*
The interaction between innovation and sustainability is positive and statistically significant (coefficient 0.48, probability value 0.009) (p.120)
Exchange rate stability supports recovery (coefficient 0.19, probability value 0.021) (p.120)
Table 3 (p.126): GDP per capita 0.22 0.10 2.10 0.051
Table 4 (p.126): CO₂ proxy 0.38** 0.31* 0.46** 0.69 Alternative sustainability measure

out_of_sample_forecast.evidence: No forecasting reported; analysis 'proceeds from descriptive profiling and bivariate associations to multivariate fixed-effects estimation, followed by robustness checks' (p.124)

E1_unit_root_tests.evidence: No unit root or stationarity tests reported; methods list only descriptive statistics, correlation analysis and fixed-effects estimation (p.124)

E2_cointegration_or_long_run_test.evidence: No cointegration or long-run test reported; static model: "The empirical relationship is estimated using a fixed-effects specification" (p.124)

E3_structural_breaks.evidence: No COVID-19 break dummy or break test reported despite sample covering 'pre-shock conditions, the disruption period, and subsequent recovery' (p.124)

E4_cross_sectional_dependence_or_heterog.evidence: Single-country annual series: 'Annual data for 2010–2024 are compiled' for Jordan (p.120); model indexed by t only

E5_endogeneity_or_omitted_variables_addr.evidence: Internal validity is improved through the inclusion of macroeconomic controls to reduce confounding from general economic trends (p.124); no IV/GMM

E6_diagnostics_stability.evidence: Diagnostics named (VIF, Shapiro–Wilk, Breusch–Pagan, Durbin–Watson) with 'key assumptions for linear estimation were adequately satisfied' (p.124-125), but no statistics reported

E7_data_source_and_period.evidence: Annual data for 2010–2024 are compiled from the United Nations World Tourism Organization, the World Bank World Development Indicators, the Jordan Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities (p.120)

notes: Tourism is the outcome (recovery index) rather than a regressor, so no tourism->sustainability coefficient. 'Fixed-effects' model is applied to a single-country annual series indexed only by t (about 15 years implied but n_obs not reported), so unit fixed effects are not identifiable as described; small-sample concerns with 6 regressors plus interaction. Composite INN and SUS index construction (weights) not reported. Robustness Table 4 notes column labels 'Lagged Tourism Recovery Index (TRI) (t-1)' as persistence check while text says lagged innovation. Diagnostics described but not quantified.
